sentences.text: Researchers compared 51 people with obsessive-compulsive disorder (39 men) to 59 healthy controls (37 men) to examine how the cerebellum connects with the rest of the brain.
Using computer simulations of brain damage and network grouping techniques, the team investigated which cerebellar parts support goal-directed versus habitual behavior.
The analysis revealed that the Crus I/II region groups with networks for goal-directed actions, while lobules V/VI group with networks for habitual actions.
In both groups, removing the Crus I/II area disrupted network coordination, but removing lobules V/VI had this effect only in the healthy controls.
People with OCD showed stronger connections within the brain's habitual action network, and this strength was linked to how severe their compulsive symptoms were.
